sentences.text: Tanius possessed a flat, elongated head featuring large openings above the temples and a narrow cheekbone.
Its vertebrae had spinous processes that were 3.2 times taller than the vertebral body.
The top surface of the third metatarsal bone displays a distinct crescent moon profile.
Gregory S. Paul once estimated this dinosaur to be 7 meters long and weigh 2 metric tons.
Fossils of at least 20 individuals of various ages have been uncovered, suggesting a significant local population.
H. C. T'an discovered the remains in April 1923 at Ch'ing-kang-kou village, located ten kilometers southeast of Lai Yang in Shandong.
The type species Tanius sinensis was formally named and described by Carl Wiman in 1929.
The genus name honors Chinese paleontologist Tan Xichou, while the species name refers to China.
Although the original specimen was largely complete, only parts could be salvaged during the excavation.
The holotype consists of the back of a flat, elongated skull.
Tanius shared its environment with Pinacosaurus, Micropachycephalosaurus, intermediate sauropods, coelurosaurs, and cheloniids.
Multiple localities of dinosaur eggs have been identified in the same formation as Tanius.
Hadrosaur carcasses, including Tanius, were trapped and moved by a mudflow event before rapid burial.
Tanius is a genus of hadrosauroid dinosaur.
It is classified within the family Hadrosauridae.
Recent analyses place Tanius as a basal member of Hadrosauridae, while others suggest it is even more basal within the broader Hadrosauroidea.
Tanius lived in China during the Late Cretaceous period.
It lived approximately 72 million years ago during the Campanian stage in what is now Asia.
Tanius lived in a fluvial to lacustrine environment within the Jiangjunding Formation.
The climate where Tanius lived was generally warm and humid, though it began to dry out after the Jiangjunding Formation, which dates to the Campanian stage.
A 2017 study by Zhang et al. determined that T. sinensis and T. chingkankouensis are valid species, while T. laiyangensis is likely invalid.
A 2019 study re-assessed "Tanius" laiyangensis as a member of the Asian saurolophine clade Kritosaurini.
